newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore to see European growth rates to mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: Singapore to see European growth rates to mid-1997.

text.p: Singapore will see low growth rates similar to levels in Europe over the next six months due to weakness in the global electronics industry, but will rebound by mid-1997 to a faster expansion, economists said on Wednesday.

"Singapore is facing a cyclical downturn which will briefly push growth rates down to unusually low levels -- levels more associated with the economies of Europe than the faster-paced, developing countries of Southeast Asia," said Paul Schymyck, economist at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce in Singapore.
"But the economy has shown in the past it can rebound sharply and it would be difficult for the island to stay out of synch with the rest of the region for very long."

The government announced late on Tuesday a relatively meagre 3.2 percent year-on-year rise in gross domestic product (GDP) for the third quarter of 1996, down from 7.5 percent in the second quarter and 11.4 percent in the first quarter.

It forecast the country's growth of around 6.0 percent for the year, after a more vigorous 8.8 percent in 1995 and 10.2 percent in 1994. The forecast implies growth of about 1.9 percent in the fourth quarter.
The government also cut its growth forecast for 1997 to between five and seven percent.
The official figures show clearly for the first time the impact of the global slump in demand for electronics and computer products, on which Singapore is heavily dependent.
Electronics accounts for around 45 percent of the city-state's manufacturing industry and close to 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
A slump in demand for electronics components in the United States and across Asia earlier in the year produced a sharp fall in Singapore's non-oil exports from June onwards.
Although demand for electronics goods worldwide has now picked up, it is likely to take another six months before this is translated into higher growth in Singapore, economists say.
"There will be more pain before there's much gain," said Prasenjit Basu, regional macro-economics director at Union Bank of Switzerland. "Growth in the first half of 1997 will be weak."
UBS expects the Singapore economy to expand by only around 2.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997 before recovering towards four to five percent growth in the second quarter.
Desmond Supple, Singapore economist at Independent Economic Analysis, said the descent to European-type growth levels of just two to three percent would be temporary this time.
"We will see a return to brisk rates of growth in the second half of 1997," he said.

But he said the island, which now enjoys a very high standard of living with accompanying high labour and raw material costs, would eventually see its growth rates fall permanently to the much slower rates seen in the developed West.
"In the next decade, probably by around 2010, Singapore's growth rates will converge with those in the West," Supple said.
